docs.title: Installation & Setup
docs.text: This guide will help you set up your machine to run mlflow-experience.

docs.title: 1. Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Python: Version 3.11 or 3.12 (Python 3.12 recommended).
  • uv: We recommend uv because it installs dependencies in seconds and manages virtual environments automatically.
  • Git: To clone the repository.
  • Docker (Optional): Required only if you want to run the self-hosted MLflow + PostgreSQL + MinIO stack. You can also run MLflow locally without Docker!

docs.title: 2. Clone the Repository
docs.text:
Open your terminal and clone the repository:

git clone https://github.com/sid-146/mlflow-experience.git
cd mlflow-experience

docs.title: Option A: Using uv (Recommended)
docs.text:
If you have uv installed, simply run:

uv sync

This single command will: 1. Create a .venv virtual environment if it doesn't already exist. 2. Install all required packages pinned in uv.lock.

To install uv if you don't have it yet: 

# Windows (PowerShell)
powershell -ExecutionPolicy ByPass -c "irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | iex"

# macOS / Linux
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh

docs.title: Option B: Using Standard pip
docs.text:
If you prefer using standard Python venv and pip:

Windows (PowerShell)macOS / Linux 
python -m venv .venv
.\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
pip install -r requirements.txt

python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt

docs.title: 4. Verify Your Environment
docs.text:
Test that the CLI tool runs and displays help:

Using uvUsing standard venv 
uv run python -m main --help

python -m main --help

You should see: 

usage: main.py [-h] --config CONFIG [--logging-level LOGGING_LEVEL]

options:
  -h, --help            show this help message and exit
  --config CONFIG       Config File Path
  --logging-level LOGGING_LEVEL
                        Debug Level

docs.title: 5. Setting up MLflow
docs.text: You have two simple choices for MLflow tracking:

docs.title: Choice 1: Run MLflow Locally (Zero Docker Needed)
docs.text:
You can run an MLflow server directly in a separate terminal:

uv run mlflow server --backend-store-uri sqlite:///mlflow.db --default-artifact-root ./mlruns --port 5000

Open http://localhost:5000 in your browser. All your experiment runs and metrics will show up here.

docs.title: Choice 2: Run via Docker Compose
docs.text:
If you have Docker Desktop installed and want a production-like stack with PostgreSQL and MinIO S3 storage:

docker compose up -d
  • MLflow UI: http://localhost:5000
  • MinIO Storage Console: http://localhost:9001 (User: minioadmin, Pass: minioadminpass)

docs.title: Project Tour
docs.text: This guide gives you a clear map of the repository so you know exactly where everything lives and what each file does.

docs.title: High-Level Directory Layout
docs.text:
mlflow-experience/
├── configs/            # Experiment YAML files
├── data/raw/           # Datasets (CSV, Excel, etc.)
├── docs/               # Documentation website source files
├── src/                # Core Python package
│   ├── orchestrator.py # Central conductor of the pipeline
│   └── core/           # Submodules (context, handlers, pipelines, trackers, logging)
├── main.py             # Entrypoint script with CLI argument parser
├── compose.yaml        # Docker Compose configuration for MLflow tracking stack
├── Dockerfile          # Container build file
├── mkdocs.yml          # Documentation site configuration
├── pyproject.toml      # Project metadata & dependencies managed by uv
└── uv.lock             # Deterministic dependency lockfile

docs.title: 1. Root Files
docs.text:
• main.py: The CLI entrypoint. It parses the --config and --logging-level flags, loads the configuration, and executes the Orchestrator.
  • compose.yaml: Defines Docker services for running the full MLflow tracking stack (PostgreSQL database, MinIO S3 object storage, and MLflow server).
  • pyproject.toml & uv.lock: Managed by uv. Defines pinned dependencies including mlflow, scikit-learn, pydantic, pandas, xgboost, and mkdocs.
  • mkdocs.yml: Configures the documentation website theme, plugins, and navigation structure.

docs.title: 2. configs/ — Experiment Definitions
docs.text: All experiments are declared in YAML. You never need to hardcode feature names or model types in Python. - configs/mvp.yaml: The working baseline configuration. Trains a Logistic Regression model on customer churn. - configs/mvp_xgboost.yaml: Same preprocessing, but trains an XGBoost classifier with custom tree hyperparameters. - configs/preprocessing.yaml: A comprehensive reference demonstrating advanced preprocessing (binning, filtering, outlier clipping, etc.).

docs.title: 3. data/raw/ — Datasets
docs.text: Stores the raw tabular data files: - churn_train.csv: 400,000+ records of telecom customer behaviors with churn labels. - churn_test.csv: Holdout test set.

docs.title: src/orchestrator.py
docs.text: The most important file in the project. The Orchestrator is a Python context manager (with Orchestrator(...) as orch:). It connects all components: 1. build(): Loads data, splits into train/test, builds transformers, and builds the Scikit-Learn Pipeline. 2. train(): Fits the pipeline on the training split and calculates training metrics. 3. test(): Predicts on the test split and calculates holdout metrics. 4. __exit__(): Automatically uploads the runtime log file to MLflow artifacts.

docs.title: src/core/context/
docs.text: Manages configuration schemas and data validation via Pydantic v2: - contexts.py: Defines the RunContext root model and sub-contexts (ProjectContext, MlFlowContext, DataContext, PreprocessingContext, ModelContext, EvaluationContext). - policies.py: Defines column-level policies (RenamePolicy, TypeCastPolicy, MissingValuePolicy, EncodingPolicy, ScalingPolicy, DatasetPolicy).

docs.title: src/core/constants/
docs.text: Lookup registries that connect YAML strings to Python classes: - registry.py: Maps strings to transformer classes (PreprocessingRegistry) and model classes (ModelType). - constants.py: Literal types for supported file formats (csv, parquet, excel) and imputation strategies.

docs.title: src/core/handler/
docs.text: Handles I/O: - config/loader.py: Loads and parses YAML files via yaml.safe_load. - data/loader.py: Finds and reads data files into Pandas DataFrames, dropping target columns to produce X and y. - data/splitter.py: Wraps Scikit-Learn's train_test_split to safely partition X and y.

docs.title: src/core/pipelines/
docs.text: Constructs the Scikit-Learn pipeline: - preprocessing.py: Iterates through the steps in context.preprocessing and instantiates matching transformer instances. - transformers.py: Contains custom Scikit-Learn transformers (RenameColumnsTransformer, MissingValueTransformer, CleaningTransformer, FilterTransformer, ScalingTransformer, EncodingTransformer). - model_builder.py: Instantiates the model estimator (e.g. LogisticRegression or XGBClassifier) with the user's hyperparameters. - evaluation.py: Helper for computing accuracy, F1 score, and other metrics.

docs.title: src/core/trackers/
docs.text: • mlflow_tracker.py: Wrapper around the MLflow client. Handles creating experiments, starting runs, logging parameters, metrics, models, and artifacts.

docs.title: src/core/logging/ & src/core/logs/
docs.text: • logger.py: Sets up two logging handlers: colorized output to your terminal, and persistent timestamped log files saved in src/core/logs/.

docs.title: Quickstart Guide
docs.text: This guide walks you through running your first machine learning experiment and viewing the results.

docs.title: Step 1: Check the Sample Data
docs.text:
The repository includes a ready-to-use customer churn dataset in data/raw/: - data/raw/churn_train.csv: Training dataset containing 400,000+ customer records. - data/raw/churn_test.csv: Holdout testing dataset.

Columns in this dataset include: - CustomerID: Customer identifier. - Age, Gender, Tenure: Demographics. - Usage Frequency, Support Calls, Payment Delay: Usage statistics. - Subscription Type, Contract Length, Total Spend: Account features. - Churn: The target column (1 = churned, 0 = retained).

docs.title: Step 2: Inspect the Configuration
docs.text: Take a look at configs/mvp.yaml. It defines: 1. Experiment Name: customer_churn_experiments 2. Data: Loads data/raw/churn_train.csv, marks Churn as target, and splits 20% for testing. 3. Preprocessing: - Renames columns to lowercase snake_case. - Casts Age, Gender, and Tenure types. - Imputes missing Age with the mean and missing Gender with the mode. - Encodes Gender and Contract Length ordinally, and Subscription Type via one-hot encoding. - Standardizes Age and min-max scales Total Spend. 4. Model: Fits a LogisticRegression classifier with max_iter: 250. 5. Evaluation: Computes accuracy and f1 score.

docs.title: Step 3: Run the Experiment
docs.text:
Run the pipeline using main.py:

Using uvUsing active virtual environment 
uv run python -m main --config configs/mvp.yaml --logging-level DEBUG

python -m main --config configs/mvp.yaml --logging-level DEBUG

docs.title: CLI Options Explained
docs.text:
• --config (required): Path to the YAML file.
  • --logging-level (optional, default: INFO):
  • Use DEBUG if you want to see detailed step-by-step diagnostic logs.
  • Use INFO for standard progress logs.
  • Use WARNING or ERROR for quiet execution.

docs.title: How to Encode Categorical Features
docs.text: Machine learning models require numerical input. This guide shows how to transform text and category columns into numerical features using one-hot and ordinal encoding.

docs.title: The Scenario
docs.text: You have columns with string or categorical values, such as: - Nominal categories (no natural order): department ("Sales", "Engineering", "HR"), city ("NYC", "London", "Tokyo"). - Ordinal categories (meaningful ranking): education ("High School", "Bachelor", "Master", "PhD"), risk_level ("Low", "Medium", "High").

docs.title: Supported Encoding Strategies
docs.text: Strategy Transformer When to Use one_hot Scikit-Learn OneHotEncoder Categories without ordering. Automatically ignores unseen categories at inference (handle_unknown="ignore"). ordinal Scikit-Learn OrdinalEncoder Categories with a specific hierarchical or natural order.

docs.title: Step 1: Configure Encoding in YAML
docs.text:
Add an encoding step under the preprocessing section in your YAML configuration:

preprocessing:
  - name: encode_categorical_features
    type: encoding
    params:
      columns:
        # 1. One-Hot Encoding for nominal columns
        - name: department
          strategy: one_hot

        - name: country
          strategy: one_hot

        # 2. Ordinal Encoding for ranked columns
        - name: customer_tier
          strategy: ordinal
          order: ["Bronze", "Silver", "Gold", "Platinum"]

        - name: experience_level
          strategy: ordinal
          order: ["Junior", "Mid", "Senior", "Lead"]

docs.title: How It Works Under the Hood
docs.text:
1. One-Hot Encoding:
  2. Converts each unique category into a binary column (0 or 1).
  3. If a new unseen category appears during testing or inference, it is assigned all zeros (handle_unknown="ignore"), preventing pipeline crashes.
  4. Ordinal Encoding:
  5. Maps each label to an integer based on the explicit order you define:
    • "Bronze" → 0.0
    • "Silver" → 1.0
    • "Gold" → 2.0
    • "Platinum" → 3.0
  6. Remainder Passthrough:
  7. Any column not listed in the columns block is untouched and passed directly to subsequent pipeline steps (remainder="passthrough").

docs.title: Pipeline Execution Order Best Practice
docs.text:
Always place missing value imputation before categorical encoding if your categories contain missing (NaN) values:

preprocessing:
  # 1. First impute missing values with the most frequent category
  - name: impute_categories
    type: missing
    params:
      columns:
        - name: department
          strategy: mode

  # 2. Then encode clean categories into numbers
  - name: encode_categories
    type: encoding
    params:
      columns:
        - name: department
          strategy: one_hot

docs.title: Step 2: Run Your Pipeline
docs.text:
uv run python -m main --config configs/my_experiment.yaml --logging-level INFO

The preprocessed DataFrame will automatically retain Pandas column labels so you can inspect feature transformations clearly in the logs.

docs.title: How to Clean Values and Filter Rows
docs.text:
Raw datasets are rarely clean. They often contain inconsistent casing, legacy abbreviations, spelling errors, or invalid rows (e.g., negative ages or test accounts).

This guide shows how to clean values and filter rows directly in your YAML configuration.

docs.title: The Scenario
docs.text: Suppose your raw dataset has: 1. Inconsistent labels in gender: "M", "F", "Male", "Female". 2. Typos in status: "actv" instead of "active". 3. Erroneous records: Rows where age <= 0 or income < 0.

docs.title: Step 1: Replace Inconsistent Values (cleaning)
docs.text:
The cleaning step applies a dictionary replacement to specific columns using Pandas replace().

Add a cleaning step under preprocessing:

preprocessing:
  - name: standardize_text_values
    type: cleaning
    params:
      replacements:
        gender:
          "M": "Male"
          "F": "Female"
        status:
          "actv": "active"
          "inactv": "inactive"
        country:
          "USA": "United States"
          "US": "United States"
          "UK": "United Kingdom"

Any value not in the dictionary remains unchanged.

docs.title: Step 2: Remove Invalid Rows (filter)
docs.text:
The filter step applies a Pandas query expression to remove invalid rows from your dataset.

Add a filter step under preprocessing:

preprocessing:
  - name: remove_invalid_rows
    type: filter
    params:
      condition: "age > 0 and income >= 0 and status != 'TEST'"

docs.title: Supported Query Syntax
docs.text:
The condition string accepts standard Pandas query syntax: - Comparison: >, <, >=, <=, ==, != - Logical operators: and, or, not - Membership: country in ['United States', 'Canada', 'Mexico'] - String matching: status != 'DELETED'

Pipeline Order Recommendation

Always place filter and cleaning steps at the very top of your preprocessing pipeline. This ensures missing value imputers, encoders, and scalers only compute statistics on clean, valid data.

docs.title: Complete Preprocessing Example
docs.text:
Here is how cleaning and filtering fit into a complete preprocessing workflow:

preprocessing:
  # 1. Clean inconsistent strings
  - name: standardize_categories
    type: cleaning
    params:
      replacements:
        gender:
          "M": "Male"
          "F": "Female"

  # 2. Filter bad records
  - name: remove_bad_rows
    type: filter
    params:
      condition: "age >= 18 and income > 0"

  # 3. Impute missing values
  - name: impute_missing
    type: missing
    params:
      columns:
        - name: income
          strategy: median

  # 4. Scale numeric values
  - name: scale_numbers
    type: scaling
    params:
      columns:
        - name: income
          strategy: robust

  # 5. Encode categories
  - name: encode_categories
    type: encoding
    params:
      columns:
        - name: gender
          strategy: one_hot

docs.title: Step 3: Run the Pipeline
docs.text:
uv run python -m main --config configs/my_experiment.yaml --logging-level INFO

The pipeline will clean dirty values, drop invalid records, and train your model on sanitized data.

docs.title: How to Train on Your Own Dataset
docs.text: This guide shows you how to plug in your own CSV, Excel, or JSON dataset into mlflow-experience without writing any Python code.

docs.title: The Scenario
docs.text: You have a new dataset (e.g. data/raw/housing.csv or data/raw/employees.csv) and want to train a model on it.

docs.title: Step 1: Place Your Data in data/raw/
docs.text:
Copy your raw dataset file into the data/raw/ directory:

# Example
cp /path/to/my_data.csv data/raw/my_data.csv

docs.title: Step 2: Create a New YAML Configuration File
docs.text:
Create a new file in configs/, for example configs/my_data.yaml:

project:
  name: my_custom_project
  owner: analytics_team
  environment: development
  description: Predicting target variable for custom dataset

mlflow:
  experiment_name: my_custom_experiments
  tracking_uri: http://localhost:5000
  track_params: true
  track_metrics: true

dataset:
  dataset_name: custom_dataset_v1
  random_state: 42
  train_test_split: 0.2  # 80% train, 20% test

  train:
    type: csv                    # "csv", "excel", or "json"
    path: data/raw/my_data.csv   # Path to your file
    id_column: id                # Primary key / ID column (excluded from training)
    target_column: target        # The column you want to predict

preprocessing:
  # Add your cleaning, imputation, and encoding steps here
  - name: handle_missing
    type: missing
    params:
      columns:
        - name: feature_1
          strategy: mean

model:
  type: logistic_regression
  task: 'binary:classification'
  hyperparameters:
    max_iter: 200

training:
  objective: binary:logistic

evaluation:
  metrics:
    - accuracy
    - f1

docs.title: Step 3: What If You Already Have Separate Train & Test Files?
docs.text:
If you already have pre-split train and test files (e.g. my_train.csv and my_test.csv), define both under dataset:

dataset:
  dataset_name: pre_split_data
  random_state: 42

  train:
    type: csv
    path: data/raw/my_train.csv
    id_column: user_id
    target_column: label

  test:
    type: csv
    path: data/raw/my_test.csv
    id_column: user_id
    target_column: label

When dataset.test is provided, the DataSplitter skips random splitting and evaluates directly on your test file.

docs.title: Step 4: Run the Experiment
docs.text:
uv run python -m main --config configs/my_data.yaml --logging-level INFO

The pipeline will read your data, isolate features from the target column, apply preprocessing, train the model, and print evaluation metrics!

docs.title: How to Handle Missing Data
docs.text: Missing values (NaNs or nulls) cause most machine learning models to fail. This guide shows you how to clean up missing values using column-specific strategies in YAML.

docs.title: The Scenario
docs.text: Your raw data has missing values: - age is missing on some rows (numeric, approximately normal). - salary is missing on some rows (numeric, highly skewed with outliers). - gender is missing on some rows (categorical). - referral_source is missing on some rows (categorical, where missing means "Direct").

docs.title: Strategy Selection Guide
docs.text: Column Type Data Characteristic Recommended Strategy Explanation Numeric Symmetric / Normal mean Replaces nulls with the arithmetic average. Numeric Skewed / Has Outliers median Replaces nulls with the 50th percentile (not distorted by extreme values). Categorical Frequent category expected mode Replaces nulls with the most frequent value in the column. Categorical/Numeric Specific default meaning constant Replaces nulls with a custom value (e.g. "Unknown", "None", or 0).

docs.title: YAML Configuration Example
docs.text:
Add a missing step to your preprocessing list:

preprocessing:
  - name: impute_missing_values
    type: missing
    params:
      columns:
        # 1. Use Mean for normally distributed numeric columns
        - name: age
          strategy: mean

        # 2. Use Median for skewed numeric columns
        - name: salary
          strategy: median

        # 3. Use Mode for standard categorical columns
        - name: gender
          strategy: mode

        # 4. Use Constant for columns with a custom fallback
        - name: referral_source
          strategy: constant
          fill_value: "Direct"

docs.title: How It Works During Training and Testing
docs.text:
MissingValueTransformer ensures zero data leakage:

  1. During Training (fit):
  2. The transformer calculates the mean of age (e.g. 34.2), the median of salary (e.g. $58,000), and the mode of gender (e.g. "Male") using training data only.
  3. These computed values are stored in memory inside self.fill_values.
  4. During Testing & Inference (transform):
  5. When new test data or live inference data arrives, nulls are filled with the exact values computed during training (34.2, $58,000, "Male").
  6. It never recalculates statistics on the test set!

docs.title: How to Run MLflow Without Docker
docs.text: By default, mlflow-experience is configured to connect to an MLflow server running in Docker at http://localhost:5000. However, you can track experiments completely offline on your local machine without running Docker.

docs.title: Option 1: Local SQLite Database (Recommended)
docs.text: Using a local SQLite database allows you to log parameters, metrics, and models to a single local database file (mlflow.db).

docs.title: Step 1: Update Your YAML Configuration
docs.text:
Set tracking_uri to point to a local SQLite database file:

project:
  name: offline_exploration
  owner: data_scientist
  environment: local

mlflow:
  experiment_name: local_experiments
  # SQLite tracking URI (stores data in mlflow.db in your project root)
  tracking_uri: sqlite:///mlflow.db
  track_params: true
  track_metrics: true
  track_artifacts:
    - classification_report
    - confusion_matrix

docs.title: Step 2: Run Your Experiment
docs.text:
Execute the training pipeline using uv:

uv run python -m main --config configs/my_experiment.yaml --logging-level INFO

MLflow will automatically initialize mlflow.db and log all run parameters, metrics, and artifacts locally.

docs.title: Step 3: Launch the MLflow UI
docs.text:
View your runs, graphs, and metric comparisons by starting the MLflow UI pointed at the SQLite file:

uv run mlflow ui --backend-store-uri sqlite:///mlflow.db

Open http://127.0.0.1:5000 in your web browser.

docs.title: Option 2: File-Based Tracking (mlruns Directory)
docs.text: If you prefer not to use SQLite, you can write experiment runs directly to local JSON and YAML files inside an mlruns/ directory:

docs.title: Step 1: Configure YAML
docs.text:
mlflow:
  experiment_name: file_based_experiments
  tracking_uri: file:./mlruns
  track_params: true
  track_metrics: true

docs.title: Step 2: Run Your Pipeline
docs.text: uv run python -m main --config configs/my_experiment.yaml

docs.title: Step 3: Launch the MLflow UI
docs.text:
uv run mlflow ui

Open http://127.0.0.1:5000 to inspect your runs.

docs.title: Comparison: When to Use What
docs.text: Mode Tracking URI Prerequisites Best For Docker Compose http://localhost:5000 Docker Desktop / Engine running Multi-user development, persistent PostgreSQL backend, production staging. Local SQLite sqlite:///mlflow.db None (uv run) Single-developer laptop, quick experiments, offline working, no Docker overhead. Local Files file:./mlruns None (uv run) Ephemeral prototyping, git-ignored local run folders.

docs.title: Switching Back to Docker
docs.text:
When you are ready to switch back to the shared Docker stack:

  1. Start the Docker containers: 
    docker compose up -d
  2. Set tracking_uri: http://localhost:5000 in your YAML config.
  3. Run your pipeline!

docs.title: How to Scale Numerical Features
docs.text:
Numerical features often have vastly different ranges. For example, age may range from 18 to 90, while annual_income ranges from \$20,000 to \$500,000. Without scaling, models like Logistic Regression or SVM will assign disproportionate weight to large-magnitude columns.

This guide shows how to configure feature scalers in mlflow-experience.

docs.title: Supported Scaling Strategies
docs.text: Strategy Scikit-Learn Class Best Used For Outlier Sensitivity standard StandardScaler Features with a roughly normal (bell-curve) distribution. Centers at mean = 0 and std = 1. Sensitive to extreme outliers. minmax MinMaxScaler Bounded data or when you need features strictly within the [0, 1] range. Highly Sensitive to outliers (compresses valid range). robust RobustScaler Datasets with frequent outliers (e.g., salaries, transaction amounts). Centers using median and interquartile range (IQR). Resistant to outliers.

docs.title: Step 1: Configure Scaling in YAML
docs.text:
Define a scaling step in your preprocessing list:

preprocessing:
  - name: scale_features
    type: scaling
    params:
      columns:
        # Standard scaling for normally distributed features
        - name: age
          strategy: standard

        # Robust scaling for features with heavy tails or outliers
        - name: annual_income
          strategy: robust

        - name: total_spend
          strategy: robust

        # Min-Max scaling for scores with known boundaries
        - name: satisfaction_score
          strategy: minmax

        - name: credit_rating_percent
          strategy: minmax

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
1. Grouped Execution:
  2. mlflow-experience groups all columns by their chosen strategy and applies them using Scikit-Learn's ColumnTransformer.
  3. Remainder Passthrough:
  4. Any column not explicitly listed (e.g., one-hot encoded flags or IDs) is preserved untouched via remainder="passthrough".
  5. No Data Leakage:
  6. The scaler computes statistics (mean, std, median, min, max) only on the training split. During test evaluation or inference, it applies those learned parameters without recalculating on test data.

docs.title: End-to-End Pipeline Order
docs.text:
For clean feature transformations, follow this logical sequence:

preprocessing:
  # 1. Impute missing numbers
  - name: handle_missing
    type: missing
    params:
      columns:
        - name: age
          strategy: median
        - name: annual_income
          strategy: median

  # 2. Scale numeric columns
  - name: scale_features
    type: scaling
    params:
      columns:
        - name: age
          strategy: standard
        - name: annual_income
          strategy: robust

  # 3. Encode categorical features
  - name: encode_categories
    type: encoding
    params:
      columns:
        - name: education_level
          strategy: one_hot

docs.title: Step 2: Run the Pipeline
docs.text:
uv run python -m main --config configs/my_experiment.yaml --logging-level INFO

The model will train on appropriately scaled features, boosting convergence speed and prediction quality.

docs.title: How to Switch and Tune Models
docs.text: This guide shows you how to change model algorithms (e.g. from Logistic Regression to XGBoost) and tune their hyperparameters simply by editing your YAML configuration.

docs.title: The Scenario
docs.text: You ran a baseline experiment with Logistic Regression, but now you want to test whether a gradient boosted decision tree (XGBoost) achieves higher accuracy or F1 score.

docs.title: Step 1: Switch to XGBoost in YAML
docs.text:
Find the model block in your configuration file and change type from logistic_regression to xgboost:

# Before: Logistic Regression
model:
  type: logistic_regression
  task: 'binary:classification'
  hyperparameters:
    C: 1.0
    max_iter: 250
    solver: saga

# After: XGBoost Classifier
model:
  type: xgboost
  task: 'xgboost:classification'
  hyperparameters:
    n_estimators: 500       # Number of boosting trees
    learning_rate: 0.05     # Shrinkage step size
    max_depth: 6            # Maximum tree depth
    subsample: 0.8          # Fraction of samples to train each tree
    random_state: 42

Also update the training objective:

training:
  objective: xgboost:binary:classification

docs.title: For Logistic Regression (type: logistic_regression)
docs.text: Parameter Default Typical Values What It Does C 1.0 0.01, 0.1, 1.0, 10.0 Inverse of regularization strength. Smaller values = stronger regularization. max_iter 100 200, 500, 1000 Maximum solver iterations for convergence. solver 'lbfgs' 'lbfgs', 'saga', 'liblinear' Optimization algorithm (saga is recommended for large datasets).

docs.title: For XGBoost (type: xgboost)
docs.text: Parameter Default Typical Values What It Does n_estimators 100 100, 300, 1000 Number of gradient boosted trees to build. learning_rate 0.3 0.01, 0.05, 0.1 Step size shrinkage used to prevent overfitting. max_depth 6 3, 6, 10 Maximum depth of a tree. Higher values capture complex patterns but risk overfitting. subsample 1.0 0.7, 0.8, 1.0 Subsample ratio of the training instances.

docs.title: Step 3: Run the New Model
docs.text: uv run python -m main --config configs/mvp_xgboost.yaml --logging-level INFO

docs.title: Step 4: Compare Models Side-by-Side in MLflow
docs.text:
1. Open the MLflow UI at http://localhost:5000.
  2. Open your experiment (e.g. customer_churn_experiments).
  3. Check the checkboxes next to both your Logistic Regression run and your XGBoost run.
  4. Click the Compare button at the top of the table.
  5. Review the side-by-side comparison of Accuracy, F1 Score, and Hyperparameters to pick the winning model!

docs.title: Docker Compose Infrastructure
docs.text: mlflow-experience provides a production-grade MLflow tracking server setup in compose.yaml.

docs.title: 1. What Services Run in Docker?
docs.text:
graph TD
    Client[Python Pipeline / Orchestrator] -->|Port 5000| MLflow[MLflow Server]
    MLflow -->|Metadata & Metrics| Postgres[(PostgreSQL 16 DB)]
    MLflow -->|Model & Log Artifacts| MinIO[(MinIO S3 Storage)]
    User[Developer] -->|Web UI Port 5000| MLflow
    User -->|Web Console Port 9001| MinIO
  1. MLflow Server (mlflow):
  2. Web UI & REST API running on port 5000.
  3. Coordinates experiment runs, parameters, metrics, and models.
  4. PostgreSQL Database (postgres):
  5. Stores all relational metadata (experiment names, run IDs, tags, parameters, and metric histories).
  6. Initialized using init-db.sql.
  7. MinIO Object Storage (minio):
  8. S3-compatible object storage for artifacts (e.g. trained model pickles, execution log files).
  9. S3 API on port 9000, Web Console on port 9001.

docs.title: 2. Environment Settings (.env)
docs.text:
Service credentials and ports are managed in .env:

# PostgreSQL
POSTGRES_DB=mlflowdb
POSTGRES_USER=mlflow
POSTGRES_PASSWORD=mlflowpass

# MinIO
MINIO_ROOT_USER=minioadmin
MINIO_ROOT_PASSWORD=minioadminpass

# MLflow Server
MLFLOW_HOST=0.0.0.0
MLFLOW_PORT=5000

docs.title: Start in the background:
docs.text: docker compose up -d

docs.title: Check status:
docs.text: docker compose ps

docs.title: Stop the services:
docs.text: docker compose down

docs.title: 4. Web Dashboards
docs.text:
• MLflow Tracking UI: http://localhost:5000
  • MinIO Storage Console: http://localhost:9001
  • Username: minioadmin
  • Password: minioadminpass
  • Bucket name: mlflow

docs.title: 5. Don't Have Docker?
docs.text:
If you don't have Docker installed or running on your system, you don't need it! You can start a local MLflow server directly with uv:

uv run mlflow server --backend-store-uri sqlite:///mlflow.db --default-artifact-root ./mlruns --port 5000

docs.title: Logging System
docs.text: The platform includes a dual-stream logging system in src/core/logging/logger.py: 1. Interactive Console Stream: Real-time output formatted with ANSI color codes. 2. Persistent File Stream: Timestamped log files saved in src/core/logs/.

docs.title: 1. Colorized Terminal Output
docs.text:
The ColoredFormatter colors output by severity level so you can spot errors or milestones instantly:

Level Color Meaning DEBUG Blue Detailed internal diagnostic messages (data shapes, step creation). INFO Green Major milestones (data loaded, training complete, evaluation scores). WARNING Yellow Recoverable issues or fallbacks (e.g. using default split ratio). ERROR Red Failures or exceptions (e.g. unconfigured model type). CRITICAL Magenta Fatal crashes.

docs.title: 2. Setting the Log Level
docs.text:
You control the console verbosity with the --logging-level command-line flag:

# Detailed step-by-step diagnostic logs
uv run python -m main --config configs/mvp.yaml --logging-level DEBUG

# Standard progress logs (default)
uv run python -m main --config configs/mvp.yaml --logging-level INFO

# Warnings and errors only
uv run python -m main --config configs/mvp.yaml --logging-level WARNING

docs.title: 3. Persistent File Logs
docs.text:
Every execution creates a timestamped log file in src/core/logs/:

src/core/logs/
├── logs_2026_10_14_23_28.log
├── logs_2026_10_15_00_12.log
└── ...

Each log line records: 

YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS : [LEVEL] : module_name : [function_name] : line_number : message

docs.title: 4. Automatic MLflow Upload
docs.text:
When the run finishes, the Orchestrator.__exit__ method automatically takes the active log file from src/core/logs/ and uploads it to MLflow under the logs/ artifact folder:

self.mlflow_tracker.log_artifact(
    console.handlers[1].baseFilename,
    f"logs/{self.mlflow_tracker.run.info.run_name}.log",
)

You can view the full log file directly from the MLflow web UI under the Artifacts tab!

docs.title: MLflow Tracking
docs.text: mlflow-experience integrates with MLflow via MLflowTracker (src/core/trackers/mlflow_tracker.py) to give you complete visibility into every experiment run.

docs.title: 1. What Gets Tracked Automatically?
docs.text:
For every pipeline run, MLflowTracker records:

  1. Parameters:
  2. Model type and hyperparameters.
  3. Dataset paths and splitting ratios.
  4. Metrics:
  5. Training and testing scores (Accuracy, F1 Score).
  6. Artifacts:
  7. Full console and file execution logs (logs/<run_name>.log).
  8. Trained model binaries.
  9. Tags & Metadata:
  10. Project name, owner, execution environment.
  11. Git commit hash and active branch.

docs.title: 2. Viewing Results in the MLflow UI
docs.text:
1. Start your MLflow server (either via Docker or locally).
  2. Open http://localhost:5000 in your browser.
  3. You will see:
  4. Experiment List: Listed on the left (e.g. customer_churn_experiments).
  5. Run History: Table of every execution, including timestamps, durations, and metric scores.
  6. Comparison View: Select multiple runs and click Compare to see side-by-side metric charts and hyperparameter differences.
  7. Artifact Browser: Click any run and select the Artifacts tab to inspect the saved session log file.

docs.title: 3. Running MLflow Locally (Without Docker)
docs.text:
You don't need Docker to use MLflow! You can run a lightweight local MLflow tracking server directly with uv:

uv run mlflow server --backend-store-uri sqlite:///mlflow.db --default-artifact-root ./mlruns --port 5000

This creates: - mlflow.db: A local SQLite file that holds all your experiment metadata. - ./mlruns: A local directory where artifacts and models are stored.

docs.title: Or use Direct File Tracking
docs.text:
You can even configure your YAML to write directly to a local directory without starting any server:

mlflow:
  experiment_name: customer_churn_experiments
  tracking_uri: file:./mlruns

docs.title: Data Ingestion & Splitting
docs.text: This section explains how data is loaded from disk, separated into features and target labels, and split into training and test sets.

docs.title: 1. Where Does the Data Come From?
docs.text:
In your YAML configuration, you specify the data source under dataset.train:

dataset:
  dataset_name: telecom_churn_v1
  random_state: 42
  train_test_split: 0.2
  train:
    type: csv
    path: data/raw/churn_train.csv
    id_column: CustomerID
    target_column: Churn

docs.title: 2. Smart Path Finding
docs.text:
You don't need to worry about path mismatches when running the command from different directories. DataLoader resolves paths in this order:

  1. Absolute path: If given an absolute path (e.g. C:\data\train.csv), it uses it directly.
  2. Current working directory: Checks relative to where you ran the command from (os.getcwd()).
  3. Repository root: Looks up the directory tree to find the file inside the project root.

docs.title: 3. Supported File Formats
docs.text:
The DataLoader reads files into Pandas DataFrames using format readers registered in DATA_READER_FUNCTIONS:

Format Extension in YAML Pandas Reader Function CSV csv pd.read_csv Excel excel or xlsx pd.read_excel JSON json pd.read_json

docs.title: 4. Separating Features and Target ($X$ and $y$)
docs.text:
When data is loaded: 1. The target column (target_column) is identified. 2. self.y is created by taking that single target column: 

self.y = self.data[target_column]
3. self.X is created by dropping the target column: 
self.X = self.data.drop(target_column, axis=1)

docs.title: 5. Train-Test Splitting
docs.text:
DataSplitter partitions the dataset before any preprocessing happens:

  • If you provide a dedicated dataset.test file in your YAML, both files are loaded directly.
  • If you only provide dataset.train, DataSplitter calls Scikit-Learn's train_test_split: 
    x_train, x_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X,
    y,
    test_size=context.dataset.train_test_split or 0.2,
    random_state=context.dataset.random_state or 42,
)

This ensures that the test split remains completely untouched until final evaluation.

docs.title: Model Evaluation
docs.text: This document explains how model performance is evaluated and recorded in mlflow-experience.

docs.title: 1. Evaluation Stages
docs.text:
The Orchestrator performs evaluation at two distinct points during a run:

  1. Training Evaluation (In-Sample): Immediately after fitting the pipeline on the training split, orchestrator.train() predicts on $X_{train}$ and evaluates against $y_{train}$. This lets you check if the model is underfitting or overfitting.
  2. Testing Evaluation (Out-of-Sample): In orchestrator.test(), the pipeline predicts on the held-out test split $X_{test}$ and evaluates against true $y_{test}$. This provides the unbiased estimate of generalization performance.

docs.title: 2. Supported Metrics
docs.text:
Currently, evaluation calculates: - Accuracy: Proportion of correct predictions over total predictions. - F1 Score: Harmonic mean of precision and recall.

In your console output, evaluation results are formatted cleanly:

INFO : 2026-10-14 23:28:18 : orchestrator.py : [evaluate] : 146 : --- Starting Evaluation (on provided dataset) ---
INFO : 2026-10-14 23:28:18 : orchestrator.py : [evaluate] : 158 : | Accuracy  : 0.8425
INFO : 2026-10-14 23:28:18 : orchestrator.py : [evaluate] : 158 : | F1 Score  : 0.8110
INFO : 2026-10-14 23:28:18 : orchestrator.py : [evaluate] : 160 : --- Evaluation Complete ---

docs.title: 3. Configuration in YAML
docs.text:
In your experiment YAML, specify which metrics you want tracked:

evaluation:
  metrics:
    - accuracy
    - f1

docs.title: 4. How to Add More Metrics
docs.text:
To add more metrics (such as Precision, Recall, or ROC-AUC), update evaluate() in src/orchestrator.py:

from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, f1_score, precision_score, recall_score

metrics = {
    "Accuracy": accuracy_score(y_true, y_pred),
    "F1 Score": f1_score(y_true, y_pred),
    "Precision": precision_score(y_true, y_pred, zero_division=0),
    "Recall": recall_score(y_true, y_pred, zero_division=0),
}

for metric_name, score in metrics.items():
    console.info(f"| {metric_name:<10}: {score:.4f}")

docs.title: Model Building & Estimators
docs.text: The ModelBuilder class (src/core/pipelines/model_builder.py) instantiates the machine learning algorithm that forms the final step of the Scikit-Learn pipeline.

docs.title: 1. Supported Model Families
docs.text:
Models are registered in the ModelType enum in src/core/constants/registry.py:

YAML type Python Class Underlying Library logistic_regression LogisticRegression Scikit-Learn xgboost XGBClassifier XGBoost

docs.title: 2. Dynamic Hyperparameter Forwarding
docs.text: You can configure any constructor parameter supported by the model directly in YAML under hyperparameters.

docs.title: Example A: Logistic Regression
docs.text:
model:
  type: logistic_regression
  task: 'binary:classification'
  hyperparameters:
    C: 1.0                # Inverse regularization strength
    max_iter: 250         # Maximum solver iterations
    solver: saga          # Algorithm to use for optimization problem
    random_state: 42

docs.title: Example B: XGBoost Classifier
docs.text:
model:
  type: xgboost
  task: 'xgboost:classification'
  hyperparameters:
    n_estimators: 500     # Number of boosted trees
    learning_rate: 0.01   # Step size shrinkage
    max_depth: 6          # Maximum tree depth
    subsample: 0.8        # Subsample ratio of training instances
    random_state: 42

docs.title: 3. How It Is Added to the Pipeline
docs.text:
Inside orchestrator.py:

# 1. Build model step
model_step = (
    self.model_builder.build()
)  # Returns [('binary:classification', model_instance)]

# 2. Append to pipeline steps
self.pipeline_steps.extend(model_step)

# 3. Create the unified Scikit-Learn Pipeline
self.pipeline = Pipeline(self.pipeline_steps)

Because the model is just the final step in the pipeline: - Calling pipeline.fit(X_train, y_train) fits all preprocessing transformers first, then fits the model on the transformed features. - Calling pipeline.predict(X_test) runs test data through all transformers first, then outputs predictions.

docs.title: Preprocessing Pipeline
docs.text: The PreprocessingPipeline class (src/core/pipelines/preprocessing.py) turns the list of steps in your YAML file into executable Scikit-Learn transformer instances.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
1. The Orchestrator calls preprocessor.build().
  2. It loops over every step defined in your preprocessing YAML list.
  3. For each step, it looks up the matching transformer class in PreprocessingRegistry.
  4. It instantiates the transformer with the validated parameters.
  5. It returns a list of (name, transformer_instance) tuples ready to be passed to Scikit-Learn's Pipeline:
[
    ("rename_columns", RenameColumnsTransformer(...)),
    ("handle_missing", MissingValueTransformer(...)),
    ("encode_features", EncodingTransformer(...)),
    ("scale_features", ScalingTransformer(...)),
]

docs.title: The Registry Mapping
docs.text:
PreprocessingRegistry connects the string type in your YAML to the Python class:

YAML type Transformer Class Policy Model rename RenameColumnsTransformer RenamePolicy missing MissingValueTransformer MissingValuePolicy encoding EncodingTransformer EncodingPolicy scaling ScalingTransformer ScalingPolicy cleaning CleaningTransformer (dict of replacements) filter FilterTransformer (query condition string)

docs.title: Order of Execution
docs.text:
Steps execute in the exact order you define them in YAML. For example:

  1. Rename first: Standardize column names (e.g. "Total Spend" $\to$ total_spend).
  2. Handle missing values: Impute null values with mean, median, mode, or constant.
  3. Encode categories: Convert string categories into numbers.
  4. Scale numeric features: Apply standard scaling or min-max normalization.

Column Name Dependencies

If you rename a column in step 1, remember to use the new name in subsequent steps (such as imputation, encoding, and scaling)!

docs.title: Custom Transformers Reference
docs.text: All transformers in mlflow-experience live in src/core/pipelines/transformers.py. They inherit from Scikit-Learn's BaseEstimator and TransformerMixin and are designed to work seamlessly within sklearn.pipeline.Pipeline.

docs.title: Retaining DataFrame Format
docs.text:
By default, Scikit-Learn transformers convert DataFrames into NumPy arrays. This strips column names and makes debugging painful.

We enable Pandas output globally:

from sklearn import set_config

set_config(transform_output="pandas")

Every transformer takes a Pandas DataFrame as input and outputs a Pandas DataFrame with column names preserved.

docs.title: 1. RenameColumnsTransformer
docs.text: Purpose: Renames columns in the DataFrame based on a dictionary mapping.

docs.title: YAML Example
docs.text:
- name: rename_columns
  type: rename
  params:
    mapping:
      "Customer ID": customer_id
      "Total Spend": total_spend

docs.title: Python Logic
docs.text:
• fit(X, y): Does nothing (stateless). Returns self.
  • transform(X): Calls X.rename(columns=self.mapping).

docs.title: 2. MissingValueTransformer
docs.text: Purpose: Imputes missing (null/NaN) values using column-specific strategies.

docs.title: Supported Strategies
docs.text:
• mean: Fills missing values with the column mean (numerical).
  • median: Fills missing values with the column median (numerical).
  • mode: Fills missing values with the most frequent value (categorical/numerical).
  • constant: Fills missing values with a specific fill_value.

docs.title: YAML Example
docs.text:
- name: handle_missing
  type: missing
  params:
    columns:
      - name: age
        strategy: mean
      - name: gender
        strategy: mode
      - name: city
        strategy: constant
        fill_value: "Unknown"

docs.title: State Learning
docs.text:
• fit(X, y): Computes the mean, median, mode, or constant on the training set only and stores them in self.fill_values[col_name].
  • transform(X): Calls X.fillna(self.fill_values).

docs.title: 3. ScalingTransformer
docs.text: Purpose: Scales numerical columns using different scalers without writing multiple separate steps.

docs.title: Supported Strategies
docs.text:
• standard: StandardScaler() (mean = 0, variance = 1).
  • minmax: MinMaxScaler() (scaled to $[0, 1]$).
  • robust: RobustScaler() (uses median and interquartile range to handle outliers).

docs.title: YAML Example
docs.text:
- name: scale_features
  type: scaling
  params:
    columns:
      - name: age
        strategy: standard
      - name: total_spend
        strategy: minmax

docs.title: How It Works Under the Hood
docs.text: ScalingTransformer groups columns by strategy and builds a Scikit-Learn ColumnTransformer: - Columns using standard are routed to StandardScaler(). - Columns using minmax are routed to MinMaxScaler(). - Any unmentioned columns pass through untouched via remainder="passthrough".

docs.title: 4. EncodingTransformer
docs.text: Purpose: Converts categorical text columns into numbers for machine learning models.

docs.title: Supported Strategies
docs.text:
• ordinal: Uses OrdinalEncoder() with an explicit order list.
  • one_hot: Uses OneHotEncoder(sparse_output=False, handle_unknown="ignore").

docs.title: YAML Example
docs.text:
- name: encode_features
  type: encoding
  params:
    columns:
      # Ordinal: preserves rank order
      - name: contract_length
        strategy: ordinal
        order: ['Monthly', 'Quarterly', 'Annual']

      # One-Hot: creates binary dummy columns
      - name: subscription_type
        strategy: one_hot

docs.title: How It Works Under the Hood
docs.text: Columns are grouped by strategy into a ColumnTransformer. One-hot encoding creates new columns (e.g. subscription_type_Basic, subscription_type_Premium), and unmentioned columns are preserved.

docs.title: 5. CleaningTransformer
docs.text: Purpose: Replaces specific categorical values or fixes inconsistencies.

docs.title: YAML Example
docs.text:
- name: clean_categories
  type: cleaning
  params:
    replacements:
      contract:
        "month-to-month": "Monthly"
        "12 Month": "Annual"

docs.title: Python Logic
docs.text: • transform(X): Loops over the columns and applies X[col].replace(mapping).

docs.title: 6. FilterTransformer
docs.text: Purpose: Filters rows based on a query condition.

docs.title: YAML Example
docs.text:
- name: filter_valid_rows
  type: filter
  params:
    condition: "tenure >= 0 and total_spend >= 0"

docs.title: Python Logic
docs.text:
• transform(X): Calls X.query(self.condition).

(Note: Row drops are best used during initial raw data preparation so the feature matrix $X$ and target vector $y$ stay aligned).
